summary.text: Writing $v=v_2(\varphi(m))$, the proof shows by induction on prime factors that any positive $m<2^{v+1}$ is a squarefree product of distinct Fermat primes $F_j$, with $v=\sum_j2^j$. For an admissible $m<2^{2^{33}+1}$, size bounds force $v=2^{33}$, whose representation as a sum of distinct powers of two forces the sole factor to be $F_{33}$; thus $F_{33}$ is minimal when prime, while if it is composite no smaller admissible $m$ exists and the admissible power $2^{2^{33}+1}$ is minimal.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\varphi(m)
\]
denote Euler's totient function, and define
\[
a(n)=\min\{m\ge 1:2^n\mid \varphi(m)\}.
\]
We will prove the asserted value for
\[
N=2^{33}.
\]
Write
\[
F_j=2^{2^j}+1
\]
for the \(j\)-th Fermat number, so in particular
\[
F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1=2^N+1.
\]

We use the notation \(\nu_2(r)\) for the exponent of \(2\) in the prime factorization of a positive integer \(r\). Thus \(2^{\nu_2(r)}\mid r\), and if \(2^d\mid r\), then \(d\le \nu_2(r)\).

The main ingredient is the following structural lemma.

**Structural lemma.** If \(m>0\) and
\[
m<2\cdot 2^{\nu_2(\varphi(m))},
\]
then there is a finite set \(S\) of nonnegative integers such that every \(F_j\), for \(j\in S\), is prime, and
\[
m=\prod_{j\in S}F_j,
\qquad
\nu_2(\varphi(m))=\sum_{j\in S}2^j.
\]
In particular, \(m\) is a product of distinct Fermat primes.

We prove the lemma by strong induction on \(m\). If \(m=1\), take \(S\) to be empty; both the empty product and the relevant totient are \(1\), and the asserted valuation is the empty sum \(0\).

Now suppose \(m\ge 2\). Choose a prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\), let \(e\ge 1\) be its exact exponent in \(m\), and write
\[
m=p^e m',
\qquad \gcd(p,m')=1.
\]
Set
\[
v'=\nu_2(\varphi(m')).
\]
Since \(2^{v'}\mid\varphi(m')\), and \(\varphi(m')\le m'\), we have the important lower bound
\[
2^{v'}\le \varphi(m')\le m'. \tag{1}
\]
By multiplicativity of the totient on coprime factors,
\[
\varphi(m)=\varphi(p^e)\varphi(m'). \tag{2}
\]

We first show that \(p\ne2\). If \(p=2\), then
\[
\varphi(2^e)=2^{e-1},
\]
so (2) gives
\[
\nu_2(\varphi(m))=(e-1)+v'.
\]
The hypothesis of the lemma would then say
\[
2^e m'=m<2\cdot 2^{e-1+v'}=2^e2^{v'}.
\]
After cancelling \(2^e\), this gives \(m'<2^{v'}\), contradicting (1). Thus \(p\) is odd.

Put
\[
k=\nu_2(p-1).
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \(k\ge1\). Also
\[
\varphi(p^e)=p^{e-1}(p-1).
\]
The factor \(p^{e-1}\) is odd, so
\[
\nu_2(\varphi(p^e))=k.
\]
Consequently, (2) gives
\[
\nu_2(\varphi(m))=k+v'. \tag{3}
\]
Since \(2^k\mid p-1\), we also have
\[
2^k\le p-1<p. \tag{4}
\]
By the hypothesis and (3),
\[
m=p^e m'<2^{k+1}2^{v'}. \tag{5}
\]

We claim that
\[
p^e\le 2^{k+1}. \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, if instead \(2^{k+1}<p^e\), then, because \(m'>0\),
\[
2^{k+1}m'<p^e m'=m<2^{k+1}2^{v'}.
\]
Cancelling \(2^{k+1}\) would yield \(m'<2^{v'}\), again contradicting (1). This proves (6).

Next we show that \(e=1\). If \(e\ge2\), then since \(k\ge1\), we have \(k+1\le2k\), and hence, using (4),
\[
2^{k+1}\le 2^{2k}=(2^k)^2<p^2\le p^e.
\]
This contradicts (6). Therefore \(e=1\).

We now identify \(p\). Write
\[
p-1=2^k u,
\]
where \(u\) is positive and odd. If \(u\ne1\), then \(u\ge3\), so
\[
p=2^k u+1\ge3\cdot2^k+1>2^{k+1}.
\]
But \(e=1\) and (6) say \(p\le2^{k+1}\), a contradiction. Hence \(u=1\), and therefore
\[
p=2^k+1. \tag{7}
\]
Because \(p\) is prime and \(k>0\), the exponent \(k\) must itself be a power of two. For completeness, write \(k=2^j q\), where \(q\) is odd. If \(q>1\), then with \(x=2^{2^j}>1\), equation (7) becomes
\[
p=x^q+1.
\]
For odd \(q>1\), \(x+1\) is a proper divisor of \(x^q+1\), since
\[
x^q+1=(x+1)(x^{q-1}-x^{q-2}+\cdots-x+1).
\]
That would make \(p\) composite. Thus \(q=1\), so \(k=2^j\) for some \(j\ge0\), and
\[
p=2^{2^j}+1=F_j. \tag{8}
\]
Thus the prime factor selected from \(m\) is a Fermat prime and occurs only to the first power.

It remains to apply the induction hypothesis to \(m'\). We claim
\[
m'<2\cdot2^{v'}. \tag{9}
\]
If instead \(m'\ge2\cdot2^{v'}\), then by (4) and (8), \(p>2^k\), whence
\[
m=pm'>2^k(2\cdot2^{v'})=2^{k+1}2^{v'},
\]
contrary to (5). Thus (9) holds. Moreover, \(m'<m\), since \(m=pm'\), \(m'>0\), and \(p>1\). The strong induction hypothesis therefore provides a finite set \(S'\) such that all \(F_i\) with \(i\in S'\) are prime and
\[
m'=\prod_{i\in S'}F_i,
\qquad
v'=\sum_{i\in S'}2^i. \tag{10}
\]
The index \(j\) from (8) is not in \(S'\): otherwise \(F_j=p\) would divide \(m'\), contradicting \(\gcd(p,m')=1\). Hence, putting
\[
S=S'\cup\{j\},
\]
this is a disjoint union, and (8), (10), and \(m=pm'\) give
\[
m=\prod_{i\in S}F_i.
\]
Finally, by (3) and \(k=2^j\),
\[
\nu_2(\varphi(m))=k+v'=2^j+\sum_{i\in S'}2^i
=\sum_{i\in S}2^i.
\]
This completes the induction and proves the structural lemma.

We also need one elementary uniqueness fact about sums of distinct powers of two:

**Binary uniqueness lemma.** If \(S\) is a finite set of nonnegative integers and
\[
\sum_{j\in S}2^j=2^t,
\]
then \(S=\{t\}\).

Indeed, no element of \(S\) can exceed \(t\), since its individual summand would then exceed the whole sum. If \(t\notin S\), all elements of \(S\) are less than \(t\), and therefore
\[
\sum_{j\in S}2^j\le1+2+\cdots+2^{t-1}=2^t-1,
\]
a contradiction. Thus \(t\in S\). Once the summand \(2^t\) is present, all other positive summands must be absent, so \(S=\{t\}\).

We now apply these facts to the desired index \(N=2^{33}\). Let
\[
\mathcal A=\{m\ge1:2^N\mid\varphi(m)\}.
\]
First observe that
\[
B=2^{N+1}
\]
belongs to \(\mathcal A\), because
\[
\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^N. \tag{11}
\]
Thus the set whose minimum defines \(a(N)\) is nonempty.

Every \(m\in\mathcal A\) satisfies
\[
m>2^N. \tag{12}
\]
To see this, divisibility gives \(2^N\le\varphi(m)\). Since \(N>0\), this excludes \(m=1\). Thus \(m>1\), and the standard strict totient inequality \(\varphi(m)<m\) gives
\[
2^N\le\varphi(m)<m,
\]
which is (12).

We next prove the decisive assertion:

**Claim.** If \(m\in\mathcal A\) and
\[
m<2^{N+1}, \tag{13}
\]
then
\[
m=F_{33}
\quad\text{and}\quad
F_{33}\text{ is prime}. \tag{14}
\]

Let
\[
v=\nu_2(\varphi(m)).
\]
Since \(2^N\mid\varphi(m)\), we have
\[
N\le v. \tag{15}
\]
Using (13) and (15),
\[
m<2^{N+1}=2\cdot2^N\le2\cdot2^v.
\]
The structural lemma therefore supplies a finite set \(S\) such that each \(F_j\), \(j\in S\), is prime and
\[
m=\prod_{j\in S}F_j,
\qquad
v=\sum_{j\in S}2^j. \tag{16}
\]
For every \(j\),
\[
F_j=2^{2^j}+1\ge2^{2^j}.
\]
Multiplying these inequalities over \(S\) and using (16), we get
\[
m=\prod_{j\in S}F_j
\ge\prod_{j\in S}2^{2^j}
=2^{\sum_{j\in S}2^j}
=2^v. \tag{17}
\]
Combining (13) and (17) yields
\[
2^v<2^{N+1},
\]
so \(v<N+1\). Together with (15), this forces
\[
v=N. \tag{18}
\]
But \(N=2^{33}\), so (16) and (18) give
\[
\sum_{j\in S}2^j=2^{33}.
\]
By the binary uniqueness lemma,
\[
S=\{33\}.
\]
The structural lemma now says both that \(F_{33}\) is prime and that
\[
m=\prod_{j\in\{33\}}F_j=F_{33}.
\]
This proves the claim.

We finish by splitting according to whether \(F_{33}\) is prime.

Suppose first that \(F_{33}\) is prime. Since
\[
F_{33}=2^N+1,
\]
we have
\[
\varphi(F_{33})=F_{33}-1=2^N.
\]
Thus \(F_{33}\in\mathcal A\). On the other hand, (12) says every \(m\in\mathcal A\) satisfies \(m>2^N\), and because \(m\) is an integer this means
\[
m\ge2^N+1=F_{33}.
\]
Therefore \(F_{33}\) is the least member of \(\mathcal A\), and
\[
a(N)=F_{33}.
\]

Now suppose that \(F_{33}\) is not prime. By (11), \(B=2^{N+1}\) belongs to \(\mathcal A\). If some \(m\in\mathcal A\) were smaller than \(B\), the claim would imply that \(F_{33}\) is prime, contradicting the present assumption. Hence every member of \(\mathcal A\) is at least \(B\), while \(B\) itself belongs to \(\mathcal A\). Therefore
\[
a(N)=B=2^{N+1}.
\]
Since \(F_{33}>1\), its failure to be prime is equivalently its being composite.

Substituting \(N=2^{33}\), we conclude
\[
\boxed{
a(2^{33})=
\begin{cases}
F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1,&\text{if }F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\[2mm]
2^{2^{33}+1},&\text{if }F_{33}\text{ is composite}.
\end{cases}}
\]
